decomposition.reasoning: Classic Latin compound. Both trans- (across) and port- (carry) are highly productive in modern English. The learner can immediately connect port- to export, import, portable, reporter, deport, and trans- to transform, transcend, transatlantic, transgender. The morphology is transparent and the etymological decomposition matches the surface form directly.

Standard Latin compound. Both ex- (meaning "out") and port- (meaning "carry") are productive in modern English. The learner can recognize ex- in exclude, exempt, exhaust, and port- in transport, import, portable, deport. The morphemes are synchronically transparent and etymologically straightforward.

Classic Latin compound. "Important" = "im- + port- + -ant", literally "carrying in" or "that which carries weight/significance". The im- prefix (Latin in-) means "into/in"; port- is the productive Latin root meaning "carry" (found in transport, export, portable, porter, portfolio, etc.); -ant is the productive Latin agentive/causative suffix (found in servant, dominant, pleasant, etc.). The morphemes are all productive in modern English and the etymology is transparent and well-established. High confidence.

Classic Latin root-plus-suffix formation. "port-" (carry) is highly productive in English, appearing in transport, import, export, reporter, important, deportation. The suffix "-able" is a standard productive English suffix meaning "capable of being". The decomposition is transparently etymologically grounded and both morphemes are recognizable to modern speakers. A learner seeing "portable" as "port- + -able" can directly connect it to other "port-" words and understand the meaning as "capable of being carried".

Prognosis is composed of the productive Greek prefix pro- (meaning "before") and the Greek root gnosis (meaning "knowledge"). The word literally means "foreknowledge" or "knowing beforehand"—a medical prediction about a patient's future condition. Both morphemes are readily recognizable in English: pro- appears in prologue, prognosis, prophecy; gnosis appears in diagnosis, agnostic, gnostic. This is a classical Greek compound that remains transparent to modern speakers.

Greek compound: dia- (through/across) + gnos- (know/recognize) + -e (infinitive). The literal sense is "to know through" or "to distinguish by knowing". The gnos- root is productive in English (cognize, recognize, agnostic, gnostic). The dia- prefix is productive (dialog, diameter, diagnosis). High confidence because both morphemes are well-established productive elements that appear in many related English words.

The word is a transparent Greek compound: a- (not) + gnost- (know) + -ic (relating to). The root gnost- is productive in English (cognate, gnostic, diagnosis, prognosis). The decomposition aligns with the historical etymology and matches the modern meaning: "one who holds that knowledge (of certain things, especially of God) is impossible or unknowable." All three morphemes are recognizable to English speakers familiar with Greek-derived vocabulary.

Standard Greek compound formed from tele- (far, distant) and phon- (sound), both highly productive Greek roots in English. The word appears in many related forms: telepathy (tele- + path-), telecast, television. The phon- root appears in microphone, phonetics, phonology, megaphone. The French nominal suffix -e is straightforward. A learner seeing this decomposition would recognize these morpheme pieces in many other English words.

Two highly productive Greek roots combined to form a modern English word meaning "light-writing" (recording with light). Both photo- and graph- appear in many other English words (photosynthesis, photograph, photon; paragraph, graphics, biography), making this decomposition immediately useful for vocabulary learning. The morphemes remain semantically transparent: a photograph is literally a graphic/writing made with light.

Standard Greek compound with two productive roots. bio- appears in biography, biosphere, antibiotic; -log- appears in psychology, geology, logic; -y is the productive Greek nominalizing suffix seen in chemistry, history, geography. Modern English speakers easily recognize "bio-" (life) and "-logy" (study of) as meaningful parts.

Two productive Greek roots joined by their standard pattern. "bio-" appears in biology, biosphere, antibiotic; "graph-" appears in photograph, paragraph, telegram. The suffix -y nominalizes the compound. Both roots are immediately recognizable to modern English speakers and the meaning "life-writing / written account of a life" is transparent and productive.

Antibiotic is a high-confidence decomposition. anti- is a productive Greek prefix meaning "against" (found in antisocial, antifreeze, antithesis). bio- is a highly productive Greek root meaning "life" (found in biology, biography, biosphere). The suffix -tic is a Greek adjective-forming suffix (found in democratic, systematic, artistic). The compound makes semantic sense: "against life" → "a substance that kills or inhibits living organisms" (especially bacteria). All three morphemes are recognizable and productive in modern English.

Standard Greek compound with two highly productive roots. geo- appears in geology, geopolitics, geometry; graph- appears in photograph, paragraph, telegram. The -y suffix is the standard Greek nominalization forming abstract nouns. All three morphemes are immediately recognizable to modern English speakers and appear in many other English words. Learner can readily see how "geo-" + "graph-" + "-y" yields "description/study of the earth".

Both geo- and log- are highly productive Greek roots in modern English. "Geo-" appears in geography, geometry, geopolitics; "log-" appears in biology, psychology, logic, etc. The -y suffix converts the root compound into a noun meaning "the study of". This is a straightforward Greek compound with clear, learnable parts that will help a learner recognize these roots in other words.

Classic Greek compound from two highly productive roots: therm- (heat) appears in thermal, thermostat, thermodynamics; meter- (measure) appears in barometer, speedometer, kilometer. Both roots are immediately recognizable to English speakers. The -o- is the standard Greek connective vowel joining the two roots. This is a textbook example of a decomposable Greek technical term that helps learners recognize the "measure heat" logic underlying the word.

Television is a straightforward compound of the Greek prefix tele- (far, distant) and the Latin root vis- (see, sight), which combines with the Latin suffix -ion to form "vision" (the act of seeing). Both tele- and vis- are productive in modern English: tele- appears in telephone, telepathy, telescope; vis- appears in video, visible, visual, revision. The morphemes are semantically transparent (far + seeing = seeing from a distance) and would be recognizable to modern English speakers. High confidence.

Both morphemes are productive in modern English. "micro-" is a very common prefix (microphone, microbe, microwave), and "scope" (from Greek skopein, "to look/examine") appears in many compound words (telescope, periscope, stethoscope, horoscope). The compound literally means "small-looker" or "an instrument for looking at small things". The decomposition is transparent to English speakers and learners can readily find other words with both morphemes.

autograph is a straightforward Greek compound: auto- (self, productive in automobile, autonomous, autocrat) + graph- (write/record, productive in photograph, paragraph, telegram) + -y (noun-forming suffix). Both roots are highly productive in modern English, and the compound meaning "one's own signature/handwriting" directly reflects the morpheme combination. No false etymologies or opaque metaphors.

Standard Greek compound. Cardi- (heart) is productive in English (cardiac, cardiograph, cardiologist) and log- (study of) is highly productive (-logy appears in biology, psychology, geology, etc.). The connective vowel -o- is the standard Greek pattern between roots. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. A learner can recognize these morphemes in many other words, making this a classic high-confidence decomposition.

Classic Greek medical compound. "derm-" (skin) is a highly productive root appearing in epidermis, hypodermic, dermatitis, etc. "log-" (study of) is equally productive, appearing in biology, psychology, geology, etc. The connective vowel "-a-" is standard in Greek compounds. The -y suffix nominalizes the root compound to mean "the study of skin." All four morphemes are recognizable and productive in modern English, making this straightforward to teach and learn.

Pediatric is a straightforward Greek compound: paed- (child) + iatr- (physician/heal) + -ic (adjective suffix "relating to"). Both roots are highly productive in English (paed- appears in pedagogy, pedantic; iatr- appears in psychiatry, geriatrics). The word is transparently decomposable and learning this morphology helps the student recognize these roots in related medical and educational terminology.

Two highly productive Greek roots (dem- appears in epidemic, endemic, demography; crat- appears in aristocrat, autocrat, bureaucrat) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound to mean "system/state of rule by the people". Both roots are immediately recognizable to English speakers and appear in many other common words.

Two productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-. Both phil- (love) and soph- (wisdom) appear in many other English words: phil- in philanthropist, bibliophile; soph- in sophomore, sophisticated. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. Emit -o- as a separate morpheme so both roots remain individually visible to the learner.

decomposition.meaning: state of, practice of, quality of

decomposition.reasoning: Philanthropy is a well-established Greek compound meaning "love of humankind". Both phil- (love, appearing in philosophy, bibliophile) and anthrop- (human, appearing in anthropology, anthropomorphic, misanthropy) are productive roots in modern English. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. This is a classic, transparent Greek formation that a learner can immediately connect to other words containing these same roots.

The word breaks into the productive Greek root chron- (meaning "time") and the common adjectival suffix -ic (meaning "relating to"). This yields the sense "relating to time" or more specifically "lasting a long time / occurring over a long period". The chron- root is highly productive in modern English (chronology, synchronize, anachronism) and -ic is one of the most common Greek-derived adjective suffixes in English. This is a straightforward, learnable decomposition.

Standard Greek compound noun. Both chron- (appearing in chronology, synchronize, anachronism, chronic) and log- (appearing in biology, psychology, geology, logic) are productive Greek roots in English. The connective vowel -o- is typical in Greek compounds. The -y suffix forms an abstract noun meaning "study of" or "the ordering/record of", as in biology, geology, psychology. This is a classic and helpful decomposition for English vocabulary learners.

Synchronize is a productive Greek-derived word. The prefix syn- (together, with) is common in English (synthesis, symphony, synchronize). The root chron- (time) is highly productive and appears in chronology, chronic, anachronism. The suffix -ize (make/cause to become) is extremely productive. Together they form "make [things happen] together in time" = synchronize. All three components are recognizable to modern English speakers and appear in many other words.

Hydrogen is a straightforward Greek compound: hydro- (water, from hydōr) + -gen (birth/origin, from genos). The root gen- is highly productive in English (genesis, genetics, pathogen, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen). The etymology is transparent: hydrogen literally means "water-producer" or "water-former," reflecting its discovery as the substance that forms water when burned. Both morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English.

decomposition.meaning: producer, producer of, that which generates

decomposition.reasoning: Oxygen is a productive Greek compound (oxy- + -gen). The oxy- root meaning "sharp/acidic" was chosen by Lavoisier because he believed oxygen was the principle of acidity; -gen is a highly productive suffix meaning "producer" or "that which generates" (seen in hydrogen, nitrogen, pathogen, allergen, etc.). Both morphemes are synchronically transparent and productive in modern English scientific terminology.

Genesis is a well-known Greek word meaning "origin" or "coming into being." The root gen- (birth, origin) appears productively in many English words: genetics, pathogen, hydrogen, genesis. The suffix -esis is a Greek nominalization suffix forming abstract nouns from verb roots, seen in words like nemesis, catharsis, synthesis. The decomposition is transparent and historically sound.

Decomposable as Latin dict- (say/tell, as in dictate, predict, diction, verdict) + -ary (relating to / collection of, as in library, vocabulary, military). The -ary suffix here means "collection of" (words with their definitions). Both morphemes are productive in modern English and the metaphor is transparent: a dictionary is a collection of words (things that are "said"). High confidence.

Standard Latin compound. pre- is a productive prefix (predict, prepare, prefix, predict) and dict- is a productive root in English (dictate, diction, prediction, verdict, dictionary). The word transparently means "say beforehand" and both morphemes are immediately recognizable to modern English speakers. This decomposition would help a learner see predict in the same family as dictate, diction, and words with the pre- prefix like prepare and predict.

Straightforward Latin compound: contra- (against) + dict- (say/speak). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. The prefix appears in contradict, contrary, contract, contraception. The root dict- appears in dictate, predict, verdict, diction, dictionary. A learner can immediately recognize these parts in other words.

Verdict is a Latin compound meaning "a spoken truth" (ver- + dict-), from Latin vēre dictum. Both roots are productive in modern English: ver- appears in "verify", "verity", "aver"; dict- appears in "dictate", "predict", "diction", "verdict", "dictionary". The compound is historically transparent and the individual morphemes are immediately recognizable to English learners as meaningful units. This is a classic example of a learnable decomposition that reveals etymology.

Manuscript is a straightforward Latin compound: manu- (hand) + script- (write). Both roots are productive in modern English (manu- appears in manual, manufacture, manicure; script- appears in describe, prescribe, manuscript). The word literally means "written by hand" and the decomposition is transparent and useful for vocabulary learning.

Standard Latin compound: de- (a productive prefix meaning "down/away") + scrib- (a productive Latin root meaning "write", found in prescribe, subscribe, manuscript, ascribe, etc.) + -tion (a productive suffix forming nouns from verbs, meaning "the process or result of"). The decomposition is transparent and all three morphemes are productive in modern English. A learner can recognize these parts in many other words.

Straightforward Latin compound: in- (productive prefix meaning "in/into") + scrib- (productive Latin root appearing in describe, prescribe, manuscript, scribe) + -tion (productive suffix for nominalization). The word means "the act of writing in/on (something)", and all three morphemes are readily recognizable in modern English (compare inscribe, inscribed, subscribe, description, etc.). High confidence.

Psychology is a transparent Greek compound: psych- (mind) + -o- (connective vowel) + log- (study/discourse) + -y (nominalizing suffix). Both psych- and log- are highly productive in modern English: psych- appears in psychiatry, psychosis, psychotherapy; log- appears in biology, geology, logic, catalogue. The meaning "study of the mind" is clear and the morphemes can be found in many other English words. This is a textbook high-confidence decomposition.

decomposition.meaning: relating to, of the nature of

decomposition.reasoning: Standard Latin root + adjectival suffix. The root mem- (memory) is productive in English and appears in other words like "remember", "memory", "memorable", "commemorate", "memento". The suffix -ial is a productive Latin adjective-forming suffix (see material, celestial, essential). The decomposition would help a learner recognize this family of related words and understand that "memorial" literally means "relating to memory".

Standard Latin root mem- (mindful, remembering) + suffix -ory (relating to / place for). The root mem- is productive in English, appearing in remember, memorial, commemorate, memento. The suffix -ory is also productive (laboratory, dormitory, directory). A learner can immediately recognize mem- in other words and understand the morphological pattern.

False-root trap. The word looks like it might decompose as "un-" + "cle", but this is misleading. "Uncle" is borrowed from Old French oncle, which comes from Latin avunculus (mother's brother), itself a diminutive of avus (grandfather). The "-cle" suffix in "uncle" is NOT the English diminutive "-cle" (as in article, particle, ridicule); it is part of the Latin etymon. A modern learner would be falsely led to think "un-" is a productive prefix here, which would be incorrect. Refuse.

False-root trap. Although "island" looks like it might decompose as "is-" + "land", the etymology is Old English "iegland" (from ieg = island + land = land). The "s" was inserted in the 16th century by folk etymology when the word was reanalyzed under the influence of the Old Norse borrowing "isle". The "-s-" is not a productive English morpheme; it's an artifact of erroneous historical reanalysis. Teaching a learner to decompose this word would be misleading, as there is no "is-" prefix or morpheme at play.

False-root trap. The word looks like it could decompose as "butt" + "-er" (agent suffix, "one who butts"), but this is etymologically incorrect. "Butter" comes from Greek "boutyron" via Latin "butyrum", referring to the dairy product. The "-er" ending is part of the inherited stem from Latin, not an English agent suffix. Decomposing it as "butt + -er" would teach a learner a false morphological pattern.

Cryptography is a standard Greek compound: crypt- (hidden/secret) + -o- (connective vowel) + graph- (write/record) + -y (nominalize). Both roots are productive in English (crypt- appears in encrypt, decrypt, cryptic; graph- appears in photograph, biography, telegram). The meaning "hidden writing" is transparent and etymologically sound. This is a paradigm case of a well-formed Greek technical term that a learner can productively understand and apply to related words.

Clear Greek composition: xeno- (foreign) + phob- (fear) + -ia (state/condition). Both xeno- and phob- are highly productive Greek roots in English (xenophobic, phobia, claustrophobia, agoraphobia). The -ia suffix is a standard Greek nominaliser. A learner can immediately connect xeno- to "xenophobe" and "xenophobic", and phob- to numerous phobia words. This is a textbook productive Greek compound.

Classic Latin compound. The prefix omni- ("all") is highly productive in English (omnipotent, omniscient, omnibus). The root vor- ("eat/devour") is productive in words like voracious, carnivore, herbivore. The -e suffix is a Latin nominalizing ending that converts the stem into an agent noun. A learner can easily see omnivore shares omni- with omnipotent and vor- with carnivore/herbivore, making this a valuable decomposition.

Standard Latin compound. "Herb-" (plant/grass) is a productive root appearing in herbaceous, herbal, herbicide. "-vore" (eater of) is a productive suffix appearing in carnivore, omnivore, insectivore. The word decomposes transparently and the parts are meaningful to modern English speakers.

Carnivore is a transparent Latin compound: carn- (flesh) + vor- (eat/devour) + -e (agent noun). Both roots are productive in modern English: carn- appears in carnage, carnal; vor- appears in voracious, omnivore, herbivore. The -i- connective is typical in Latin compounds and should be marked separately so both roots remain clearly visible. This is a standard, uncontroversial decomposition with high confidence.

Classical Latin compound: bene- (good, well) + vol- (wish, will) + -ent (having quality of). The root vol- is productive in English (volunteer, volition, involuntary). The prefix bene- is productive (benefit, benefactor, benign). The suffix -ent is productive (student, dependent, apparent). The decomposition directly yields the meaning: "well-wishing" → "kind, charitable". This is a standard, transparent morphological formation that would help learners recognize the pattern in related words like "malevolent" (mal- + vol- + -ent) and "benign" (bene- + root).

Malevolent is a classical Latin compound: mal- (bad) + vol- (wish/will) + -ent (having quality of). Both the prefix mal- and the root vol- are productive in English: mal- appears in malfunction, malice, malformed; vol- (in the sense of willing/wishing) appears in volunteer, involuntary. The -ent suffix is a standard Latin nominative/adjectival ending used productively in English for forming adjectives (present, student, dependent, etc.). The meaning "having bad wishes" or "wishing ill" aligns directly with the morpheme composition. High confidence.

Straightforward Latin compound: re- (prefix meaning "again") + nov- (root meaning "new", as in novel, innovate, novice) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). All three morphemes are productive in modern English. The meaning "make new again" is transparent and helps learners connect to other nov- words (innovation, novelty) and other -ate verbs (create, activate, educate).
